Trips / Austria

Birding in Austria

Soda pans on the Hungarian plain, the full woodpecker set in the limestone forests, and an alpine list on a pass road above the treeline.

424species with a card here
10birding regions
Neusiedler See Marchegg Donau-Auen Rax and Schneeberg Thayatal Hohe Tauern Ehrwald Rheindelta Kalkalpen Gesause
Birds When to Go Where to Bird Itineraries Prep FAQ Community

At a glance

Best months
May for the Seewinkel and the eastern steppe, late June and July for the Alpine road, and February to April for the woodpeckers and the Ural Owls
Getting around
Austria is the easiest country on this site to bird by train. Rail reaches the Seewinkel, the Wienerwald and the Gesause, and cable cars reach the high ground. The Grossglockner road wants a car
The one thing to know
The Grossglockner Hochalpenstrasse closes for the winter and late snow can delay the reopening, so an Alpine trip is planned around the road rather than the other way round

When to Go

The Austrian year splits cleanly in two. The eastern lowlands run from late winter through spring, with the woodpeckers drumming before the bustards display, and the mountains only start once the high road opens.

spring

March to May

The lowland season. Great Bustards display on the Parndorf Plain, the Seewinkel soda pans fill with breeding waders and the forests are drumming.

Go for Great Bustard, Saker Falcon, the breeding waders and the woodpecker set.

Trade off The Alpine passes are still shut, so the mountain list is out of reach until late spring.

Typical daily average Wien 6 to 15 °C / 43 to 59 °F, Innsbruck 4 to 15 °C / 39 to 59 °F, Bregenz 4 to 12 °C / 39 to 54 °F

summer

June to August

The Alpine season. The Grossglockner road is open and the high ground holds Lammergeier, Alpine Accentor, Snowfinch and Ptarmigan.

Go for The full Alpine list, Red-footed Falcon in the Seewinkel, Spoonbill on the pans.

Trade off The soda pans dry through summer and the Alpine roads carry heavy tourist traffic.

Typical daily average Wien 14 to 25 °C / 57 to 77 °F, Innsbruck 12 to 23 °C / 54 to 73 °F, Bregenz 12 to 21 °C / 54 to 70 °F

autumn

September to October

Passage through the Rheindelta and the eastern wetlands, with the first wildfowl arriving on Lake Constance.

Go for Wader and wildfowl passage, raptors moving south.

Trade off The Grossglockner road closes for the winter, usually from late autumn.

Typical daily average Wien 8 to 17 °C / 46 to 63 °F, Innsbruck 6 to 18 °C / 43 to 64 °F, Bregenz 8 to 16 °C / 46 to 61 °F

winter

November to February

Lake Constance and the Danube hold the wintering waterbirds, and late winter starts the woodpeckers drumming and the Ural Owls calling.

Go for Wintering waterbirds, White-tailed Eagle, and the first forest song of the year.

Trade off The Alps are closed to birding and the eastern lakes can freeze.

Typical daily average Wien -1 to 5 °C / 30 to 41 °F, Innsbruck -2 to 6 °C / 28 to 43 °F, Bregenz -2 to 4 °C / 28 to 39 °F

Austria End to End

Vienna (VIE), the Seewinkel, Marchegg, the Wienerwald, the Kalkalpen, the Gesause, the Hohe Tauern, the Tyrol, the Rheindelta

East to west, lowland steppe to Alpine road to Lake Constance. Late May into June is the window when the passes are open and the lowlands are still breeding.

Neusiedler See, the Seewinkel and the Parndorf Plain

A shallow steppe lake with a reed belt kilometres wide, a scatter of soda pans behind it, and the bustard plain above

The reason most birders come to Austria. Neusiedler See is a shallow steppe lake with a reed belt kilometres wide, and the Seewinkel behind it is a scatter of soda pans that hold Avocet, Spoonbill, Red-footed Falcon and Black-tailed Godwit. The Parndorf Plain above carries Great Bustard and Saker Falcon.

  • Look for: Great Bustard, Saker Falcon, Red-footed Falcon, Pied Avocet, Eurasian Spoonbill, Black-tailed Godwit, Bearded Reedling, Moustached Warbler
  • Stops:
    • , the national park headquarters on the eastern shore, which holds the current water levels for the pans and is the place to ask which of them are wet this week
    • , the largest of the soda pans, ringed by a track that stays open to walkers, and the most reliable of them for Avocet and Spoonbill because it holds water longest
    • , wet meadow between the reed belt and the farmland at the lake's north-east corner, cut late so the Corncrake and the Great Grey Shrike hold territory through the summer
    • , a gravel plain of open arable above the lake, and the Austrian ground for Great Bustard, which winters here in the hundreds
    • , the one point where a road reaches open water through a reed belt kilometres deep, watched from the harbour wall for terns and the marsh warblers behind it
  • Also covers: Burgenland
  • Also watch for: European Souslik holds colonies on the short turf of the Parndorf Plain, which is what the Saker Falcon is there for. Konik horses and Hungarian Grey Cattle graze the pans under a conservation scheme, and European Hare is everywhere on the open ground.
Where to Stay3 places to stay

Austria is the third country in a row where the obvious scheme is the wrong one. Green Key has almost no Austrian presence, and leading on it would produce a near-empty section. What carries the country is the Österreichisches Umweltzeichen, Austria's own national ecolabel, whose tourism register lists on the order of six hundred establishments across all nine states. That figure is a count taken off the register's own listing rather than an official published total, and it is stated that way on purpose. Every property below carries a certification from a scheme's own record and sits within reach of somewhere in the regions above. What each certification actually means

The March Floodplains and Marchegg

Oak floodplain forest on the March river, carrying the largest tree-nesting White Stork colony in Europe

Marchegg holds the largest tree-nesting White Stork colony in Europe, in oak floodplain forest on the March river. The floodplain behind gives Black Stork, White-tailed Eagle and the woodpeckers, and it is forty minutes from Vienna.

  • Look for: White Stork, Black Stork, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Collared Flycatcher, Red-breasted Flycatcher, Common Kingfisher, Lesser Spotted Eagle
  • Stops:
    • , an oak floodplain forest on the Slovak border carrying the largest tree-nesting White Stork colony in Europe, with the nests visible from a signed walk out of the village
    • , the softwood forest along the river itself, flooded most springs, which is what keeps the woodpeckers and the Black Stork in it
  • Also covers: Poysdorf
  • Also watch for: European Beaver works the March itself and the oxbows behind it, Red Deer use the floodplain forest, and European Pond Turtle basks on the warm banks in spring.

Austria is the third country in a row where the obvious scheme is the wrong one. Green Key has almost no Austrian presence, and leading on it would produce a near-empty section. What carries the country is the Österreichisches Umweltzeichen, Austria's own national ecolabel, whose tourism register lists on the order of six hundred establishments across all nine states. That figure is a count taken off the register's own listing rather than an official published total, and it is stated that way on purpose. Every property below carries a certification from a scheme's own record and sits within reach of somewhere in the regions above. What each certification actually means

The Danube Wetlands and Donau-Auen

The last free-flowing stretch of the Austrian Danube, running east from Vienna as side-arms, gravel banks and softwood forest

The Danube east of Vienna runs through the last free-flowing floodplain forest on its Austrian length, protected as a national park. The wetlands here are side-arms, gravel banks and softwood forest, with Kingfisher, Black Woodpecker, White-tailed Eagle and a beaver population.

  • Look for: White-tailed Eagle, Black Woodpecker, Grey-headed Woodpecker, Black Kite, Common Sandpiper, Eurasian Golden Oriole, Syrian Woodpecker
  • Stops:
    • , the village the national park is run from, with the moated castle holding its visitor centre and the boat trips into the side-arms leaving from the bank below
    • , the cut-off meanders and backwaters of the Lobau, reached on foot or by bicycle from the city, holding Kingfisher, Black Woodpecker and the river's own warblers
    • , the stretch of unregulated riverbank the 1984 occupation saved from a dam, and the reason the national park exists
  • Also watch for: European Beaver recolonised the side-arms and is now easy to find at dusk. European Pond Turtle is the park's own flagship and has a breeding programme behind it, and Green Toad spawns in the pools left on the gravel.

Rax-Schneeberg and the Wienerwald

Two limestone summits above two thousand metres within an hour of Vienna, both reached by cable car, and the biosphere park below them

The limestone hills southwest of Vienna, and the Wienerwald biosphere park where Ural Owl was reintroduced. Rax and Schneeberg both top two thousand metres and give the Alpine species on a cable car ride rather than a two-day walk.

  • Look for: Ural Owl, Eurasian Pygmy Owl, Boreal Owl, Ring Ouzel, Water Pipit, Alpine Swift, Rock Bunting
  • Stops:
    • , the cable car that lifts you to 1,550 m in eight minutes, which is the practical way onto the plateau for Alpine Accentor and Water Pipit without a four-hour climb
    • , the summit of the Rax at 2,007 m, an open limestone plateau where Alpine Chough work the walkers and Rock Thrush hold the screes
    • , beech and oak woodland on Vienna's western edge, and the release area for the Northern Bald Ibis, which now breeds again in Austria after four hundred years
  • Also covers: Baden, Hernstein, Pöllauberg, Wien
  • Also watch for: Chamois live on the open limestone of both summits, Red Deer and Roe Deer through the Wienerwald beech, and Alpine Salamander comes out on the paths after rain.

The Waldviertel and Thayatal

Granite upland and old forest along the Czech border, with the Thaya meandering through a wooded gorge at Hardegg

The Waldviertel is granite upland and old forest along the Czech border, with Thayatal national park on the river meanders at Hardegg. Black Stork on the Thaya, and the forest woodpeckers through the surrounding woods.

  • Look for: White-backed Woodpecker, Hazel Grouse, Eurasian Three-toed Woodpecker, Northern Raven, Common Redstart, Eurasian Wryneck, Black Redstart
  • Stops:
    • , a steep wooded river gorge on the Czech border with a visitor centre in Austria's smallest town, holding nine woodpeckers in one valley
    • , the loops the river cuts through the gorge, watched from the marked trails above for Black Stork and Eagle Owl on the rock faces
    • , the medieval carp ponds of the granite plateau, drained in rotation, which is when the waders and the Black Tern arrive
  • Also covers: Purgstall
  • Also watch for: European Otter works the Thaya and its tributaries, European Wildcat is confirmed in the national park by camera trap, and Fire Salamander is common on the damp granite.

Austria is the third country in a row where the obvious scheme is the wrong one. Green Key has almost no Austrian presence, and leading on it would produce a near-empty section. What carries the country is the Österreichisches Umweltzeichen, Austria's own national ecolabel, whose tourism register lists on the order of six hundred establishments across all nine states. That figure is a count taken off the register's own listing rather than an official published total, and it is stated that way on purpose. Hohe Tauern and the Grossglockner

Austria's largest national park, crossed by a toll road that climbs to 2,504 m at the Hochtor pass

The Grossglockner Hochalpenstrasse climbs to two and a half thousand metres and is the single best Alpine birding road in the country. Lammergeier, Golden Eagle, Alpine Accentor, Snowfinch, Ptarmigan and Alpine Chough, with national park centres at Mittersill, Mallnitz and Matrei.

  • Look for: Bearded Vulture, Golden Eagle, Alpine Accentor, White-winged Snowfinch, Rock Ptarmigan, Alpine Chough, Common Rock Thrush, Citril Finch
  • Stops:
    • , a pass at 2,428 m on the Grossglockner toll road with a car park at the top, open May to October, which puts Alpine Chough, Snowfinch and the Bearded Vulture flight line a few steps from the vehicle
    • , the park's main centre in the Salzach valley, and the place that publishes where the released Bearded Vultures are currently ranging
    • , the Carinthian entrance to the park, with the Seebachtal walk behind it for Ring Ouzel, Nutcracker and Three-toed Woodpecker in the spruce
    • , the road head under the Pasterze glacier at 2,369 m, the standard vantage for Golden Eagle and Bearded Vulture over the Glockner face
  • Also covers: A- Neukirchen am Großvenediger, Alpbach, Bad Gastein, Bad Häring, Bad Hofgastein, Bischofshofen, Bramberg, Dienten am Hochkönig, Döbriach, Ebbs, Ellmau, Fieberbrunn, Flachau, Going, Hermagor, Hinterglemm, Hochfilzen, Hopfgarten im Brixental, Kaprun, Katschberghöhe, Kirchdorf in Tirol, Kleinarl, Krimml, Kufstein, Leogang, Lienz, Malta, Maria Alm, Maria Luggau, Matrei in Osttirol, Millstatt, Neukirchen am Grossvenediger, Niederau, Oberndorf in Tirol, Obertauern, Piesendorf, Rennweg am Katschberg, Saalbach, Saalfelden, Salzburg, Sankt Daniel, Sankt Martin bei Lofer, Scheffau, Söll, St Johann in Tirol, St. Jakob in Haus, St. Johann in Tirol, Tröpolach, Wagrain, Walchsee, Weissensee, Werfenweng, Wildschönau, Zell am See
  • Also watch for: Alpine Ibex and Chamois are both reliable from the road, and Alpine Marmot whistles from every scree slope above the treeline through the summer.

Tyrol, the Zugspitze-Wetterstein and Karwendel

Tyrolean limestone under the Zugspitze and the Wetterstein wall, where a cable car puts the high ground within a morning

The Tyrolean limestone around Ehrwald, under the Zugspitze and the Wetterstein wall. The cable car gives the high ground quickly, Alpine Accentor and Wallcreeper on the rock, and the Karwendel behind holds the same set with a longer walk in.

  • Look for: Wallcreeper, Northern Nutcracker, Black Grouse, Rock Partridge, Rock Ptarmigan, Eurasian Crag Martin, Red-billed Chough
  • Stops:
    • , the largest nature park in Austria, a limestone range of pine and open scree reached from the Tyrolean valleys, holding Rock Ptarmigan, Alpine Accentor and Golden Eagle
    • , the valley base under the Wetterstein, and the walk up the Ehrwalder Alm for Black Grouse at the treeline in early morning
    • , a lift-served ridge above Lermoos, searched for Rock Ptarmigan on the summit ridges and Ring Ouzel in the dwarf pine below them
    • , a deep lake in the valley floor holding Goldeneye and Goosander through the winter, with beaver sign along the outflow
  • Also covers: A- Schattwald, Grän, Innsbruck, Längenfeld, Leutasch, Mieming, Neustift im Stubaital, Obsteig, Pitztal, Seefeld, Telfs, Umhausen, Zöblen
  • Also watch for: Chamois work the ledges below the cable car stations and Alpine Marmot the alpine meadows, with Alpine Salamander on the paths in wet weather.
Where to Stay25 places to stay

Austria is the third country in a row where the obvious scheme is the wrong one. Green Key has almost no Austrian presence, and leading on it would produce a near-empty section. What carries the country is the Österreichisches Umweltzeichen, Austria's own national ecolabel, whose tourism register lists on the order of six hundred establishments across all nine states. That figure is a count taken off the register's own listing rather than an official published total, and it is stated that way on purpose. Every property below carries a certification from a scheme's own record and sits within reach of somewhere in the regions above. What each certification actually means

Rates appear only where the Wild and Worthy supplier archive publishes a band. The Green Key register carries no prices, so most rows here have none. Each band reads in US dollars, euros and pounds, converted at European Central Bank reference rates for August 2026.

The Rheindelta and Vorarlberg's Lake Constance Shore

Austria's only Lake Constance shore, where the Rhine arrives in reedbed, open water and alluvial forest

Austria's only stretch of Lake Constance, where the Rhine arrives in a delta of reedbed and alluvial forest. It is the country's most important wetland for passage and wintering waterbirds, and the Rheinholz forest behind adds the woodland species.

  • Look for: Great Crested Grebe, Common Pochard, Tufted Duck, Common Goldeneye, Water Rail, Bluethroat, Common Reed Warbler
  • Stops:
    • , the abandoned river channel on the Swiss frontier, still and reed-fringed, and the delta's best water for Bittern and Bearded Reedling
    • , the engineered mouth where the Rhine enters the lake, whose sandbanks carry the tern and gull roosts and the passage waders
    • , the wet woodland behind the reeds, which is where the delta's woodpeckers and the Golden Oriole are
    • , a tributary mouth with a hide on the reed edge, searched for crakes and for the duck flocks that gather off it in winter
  • Also covers: Bizau, Bregenz, Dornbirn, Feldkirch, Hirschegg, Lech, Riezlern, Sankt Gallenkirch, Schruns, Silbertal, St. Gallenkirch, Tschagguns, Warth, Zurs
  • Also watch for: European Beaver has returned to the Old Rhine arms, and the reserve is one of the richest dragonfly sites in the country through high summer.

Kalkalpen and the Reichraminger Hintergebirge

The largest unbroken forest wilderness in Austria, with a core zone left entirely to itself

The Kalkalpen national park protects the largest unbroken forest wilderness in Austria, and the Reichraminger Hintergebirge core zone is the reason it holds all the woodpeckers, White-backed among them. Sengsengebirge above adds the mountain birds.

  • Look for: Western Capercaillie, Eurasian Nuthatch, Boreal Owl, Eurasian Treecreeper, Willow Tit, Crested Tit, Eurasian Bullfinch
  • Stops:
    • , the largest unbroken forest wilderness in the country, left entirely to itself, which is why the full woodpecker set survives in it
    • , the limestone ridge on the park's northern edge, holding Rock Ptarmigan and Alpine Chough above the treeline and Hazel Grouse in the mountain pine below
    • , a lift-served viewpoint at the park's gateway, and the easiest place to scan the ridges for Golden Eagle
  • Also covers: Altaussee, Bad Aussee, Bad Mitterndorf, Eberstalzell, Hinterstoder, Marchtrenk, Neuhofen, Steyr, Tauplitz, Traun, Ybbs
  • Also watch for: Eurasian Lynx is present in small numbers and monitored by camera trap, Red Deer use the valley floors, and the deadwood the core zone keeps supports an exceptional beetle fauna.

Gesause and the Enns Valley

A limestone gorge cut by the Enns, with walls rising close to a thousand metres straight off the river

The Enns cuts a gorge through limestone at the Gesause, and the walls give Wallcreeper, Golden Eagle and Peregrine. The Xeis plateau above and the Hartelsgraben side valley carry the forest and mountain birds together.

  • Look for: Peregrine Falcon, White-throated Dipper, Red Crossbill, Goldcrest, Grey Wagtail, Fieldfare, Coal Tit
  • Stops:
    • , the whitewater gorge the park is named for, where the Enns cuts through limestone, holding Dipper and Grey Wagtail on the river and Wallcreeper on the walls in winter
    • , the high ground above the gorge, reached on foot, for Alpine Accentor, Water Pipit and the Rock Thrush of the open screes
    • , a steep side valley of old spruce and beech, searched at first light for Three-toed Woodpecker and Pygmy Owl
  • Also covers: Admont, Bruck an der Mur
  • Also watch for: Chamois are constant on the walls, Alpine Ibex hold a reintroduced colony on the high ground, and Red Deer come down into the Johnsbach valley at dusk.

Preparation

BeakBrain Learn the Austrian list before you travel Austria runs from steppe bustards to Alpine Snowfinch by way of nine woodpeckers, which is a wide list to meet cold. Every species here as a collector card. Learn these 424 birds before you fly
  • Birds of Europe · Lars Svensson, Killian Mullarney and Dan Zetterström. The Collins guide, the standard for the whole Western Palearctic and the one every European birder carries.
  • BirdLife Österreich · the national partner. The Austrian BirdLife partner, running the atlas and the reserve network.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Austria?

May for the lowlands and late June for the Alps, which is why a trip covering both usually runs in early June. The Seewinkel is at its best in May and the Grossglockner road needs the passes open.

Where do I go for Great Bustard in Austria?

The Parndorf Plain above the Seewinkel, and the Hansag on the Hungarian border. The birds are on farmland managed for them and are watched from the road at range, because they are protected from disturbance.

Is the Grossglockner road open all year?

No. It closes for the winter and reopens in late spring, and late snow can delay that. Check the road's own site before booking an Alpine trip around it, because there is no alternative at that height.

Which country is best for woodpeckers in Europe?

Austria has a strong claim. The Kalkalpen national park holds the largest unbroken forest wilderness in the country, and its Reichraminger Hintergebirge core zone carries the dead-wood specialists including White-backed.

Can I bird Austria without a car?

More than most countries, yes. The rail network reaches Illmitz for the Seewinkel, the Wienerwald and the Gesause, and cable cars take you onto the high ground at Rax and Ehrwald. The Grossglockner road still wants a car.

What certification should I look for in Austrian accommodation?

The Österreichisches Umweltzeichen, the Austrian Ecolabel, which is the national scheme and carries the tourism sector here. Green Key has almost no Austrian presence, so it is the wrong thing to look for.

What is the Ural Owl doing in Austria?

It was reintroduced after most of a century's absence, into the Wienerwald biosphere park and the wilderness area south of Vienna, and it now breeds. Late winter is when the birds call.

Who are the birding institutions in Austria?

BirdLife Österreich is the partner organisation and runs the rarities committee and the monitoring. The national parks at Neusiedler See, Hohe Tauern, Donau-Auen, Kalkalpen, Thayatal and Gesäuse manage most of the ground above.

Birding Community

Birding here runs through a BirdLife partner and six national parks, and the parks manage most of the ground listed above. Find a birding organisation near you in our worldwide directory

Alongside the national bodies below, Austria has 8 local bird clubs across 9 regions. They run the walks and the counts, and most of them welcome visitors. See every Austrian club by region.
